The midterms generated a blue wave that swept Republicans out of power in the House and the Senate, reversing the party’s fortunes just two years after Trump’s return to the White House. The results amounted to a decisive rebuke of a President whose handling of the economy, rising prices, and the war with Iran had fueled widespread discontent, and who spent the closing days of the campaign musing about candidates’ anatomy and dismissing Americans’ concerns over their bottom line.

For the first time since Trump returned to Washington, Democrats will be able to set the legislative agenda, compel testimony from Administration officials, investigate allegations of corruption, and force Republicans to take difficult votes. Party leaders see an opportunity to turn the public’s discontent with Trump into a sustained argument for returning Democrats to the White House in 2028.

Interviews with more than two dozen Democratic leaders, strategists, and members of Congress reveal a party itching to fight on nearly every front the President has opened. But when the midterm victory laps conclude, the Democrats’ deeper problems will be waiting for them. Even leading up to their midterm victory, surveys showed the party remains unpopular. Its leaders are divided over how far left to move, what kind of economic message will win back the voters who abandoned them in 2024, and how aggressively to confront Trump.

At the link in bio, read our new cover story on how Democrats could wield their newfound power.

Shortly afterward, he reported the interception and destruction of a drone also directed at the southern region.

Saudi authorities have occasionally reported debris from intercepted projectiles causing limited damage or minor injuries, while the Houthis have claimed attacks on airports and energy infrastructure.

Imagine a coffin remaining sealed for more than 2,500 years — then finally being opened in front of a crowd.

In October 2020, Egyptian archaeologists made headlines after opening an ancient sarcophagus at Saqqara, a historic burial site south of Cairo.

The coffin was one of 59 sealed wooden sarcophagi discovered in the area.

When the lid was lifted, researchers revealed a mummy wrapped in decorated burial linen, with colorful inscriptions still visible.

The coffins date back to Egypt’s Late Period and are believed to have belonged to priests and other prominent individuals.

The discovery offered archaeologists a remarkable glimpse into ancient Egyptian burial traditions.

More than two millennia later, the secrets of the ancient world were still being uncovered. 🏺

A sealed coffin. An ancient mummy. A discovery over 2,500 years in the making.

Democrats got walloped in 2024 and have since sought to understand why. One theory has been that Kamala Harris didn’t do enough “new media.” She didn’t go on Joe Rogan’s podcast or spend enough time in the online spaces where swing voters, young men and low-information voters increasingly get their news. There is truth to that critique. But that doesn’t mean every platform, personality or form of outreach is politically wise. Take the party’s recent flirtation with Hasan Piker.

Piker, a 34-year-old left-wing Twitch streamer, has millions of followers online. Notable progressives — including Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vermont), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York), Rep. Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — have recently sought to capitalize on his platform. The argument for engaging him, which New York Times columnist Ezra Klein recently articulated, usually goes like this: Democracy requires tough conversations. Democrats ought to engage with different voices and resist the temptation to cancel anyone. They need to expand their reach and show up in more places.

Piker certainly fits that bill, but the downside of associating with him is significant. The internet personality has described Orthodox Jews as “inbred,” said “America deserved 9/11,” asserted “Hamas a thousand times better” than Israel and called the collapse of the Soviet Union “one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century.” In a podcast interview with a former Obama speechwriter last week, he called the Republican Party the “biggest terrorist internationally.” Other Democrats have openly rejected his views. Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres (New York) called Piker “the poster child for the post-October 7th outbreak of antisemitism in America.”

The congressman is right. Piker’s rhetoric, moreover, reinforces caricatures Republicans have spent years attaching to Democrats: that they are weak, anti-American, extreme and culturally alienating.

Consider how the GOP is already punishing Democratic candidates for fraternizing with Piker.

[{'caption': "An op-ed by @EthanMWolf, founder of @DemocraticWinsMedia: 

Democrats got walloped in 2024 and have since sought to understand why. One theory has been that Kamala Harris didn’t do enough “new media.” She didn’t go on Joe Rogan’s podcast or spend enough time in the online spaces where swing voters, young men and low-information voters increasingly get their news. There is truth to that critique. But that doesn’t mean every platform, personality or form of outreach is politically wise. Take the party’s recent flirtation with Hasan Piker.

Piker, a 34-year-old left-wing Twitch streamer, has millions of followers online. Notable progressives — including Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vermont), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York), Rep. Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — have recently sought to capitalize on his platform. The argument for engaging him, which New York Times columnist Ezra Klein recently articulated, usually goes like this: Democracy requires tough conversations. Democrats ought to engage with different voices and resist the temptation to cancel anyone. They need to expand their reach and show up in more places.

Piker certainly fits that bill, but the downside of associating with him is significant. The internet personality has described Orthodox Jews as “inbred,” said “America deserved 9/11,” asserted “Hamas a thousand times better” than Israel and called the collapse of the Soviet Union “one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century.” In a podcast interview with a former Obama speechwriter last week, he called the Republican Party the “biggest terrorist internationally.” Other Democrats have openly rejected his views. Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres (New York) called Piker “the poster child for the post-October 7th outbreak of antisemitism in America.”

The congressman is right. Piker’s rhetoric, moreover, reinforces caricatures Republicans have spent years attaching to Democrats: that they are weak, anti-American, extreme and culturally alienating.

Consider how the GOP is already punishing Democratic candidates for fraternizing with Piker.

Janosch ist im Alter von 95 Jahren gestorben. 😢

Gestern habe ich noch mit meinem Enkel Ben eines seiner Bücher gelesen. Heute nehmen wir Abschied von einem Menschen, der Generationen mit seinen Geschichten begleitet hat.

Janosch, mit bürgerlichem Namen Horst Eckert, hatte keine leichte Kindheit. Sie war von Gewalt und schmerzhaften Erfahrungen geprägt. Und doch schenkte er uns Geschichten voller Wärme, Humor, Fantasie und Freundschaft.

Seine Lebensweisheiten waren geprägt von tiefem Humor, Entschleunigung und einer unprätentiösen Sicht auf das Leben.

Der kleine Tiger, der kleine Bär und die Tigerente brauchten keinen großen Reichtum, um glücklich zu sein.

Sie hatten einander.

Vielleicht ist das die schönste Botschaft seiner Geschichten:

Du hast uns nicht erklärt, wie man glücklich wird. Du hast uns gezeigt, wie wenig man dafür manchmal braucht.

Janosch hat uns gelehrt, dass Freundschaft wichtiger ist als Besitz, dass Fantasie keine Grenzen kennt und dass das Glück oft dort wartet, wo wir längst zu Hause sind.

Seine Geschichten waren nie nur für Kinder. Sie waren auch kleine Lebensweisheiten für Erwachsene.

💛 Danke, Janosch. Für das Lachen, die Wärme und die Erinnerungen.

Und dafür, dass ich deine Geschichten heute noch an meinen Enkel weitergeben darf.

❗ LACK OF TRANSPARENCY: Missing ingredient lists and safety documentation make it harder for consumers to know what they are applying to their skin.

Not every inexpensive cosmetic is unsafe, and not every regulatory violation means a product is toxic.

But low prices must never come at the expense of human health and safety!

💔 OUR SKIN IS NOT A TESTING GROUND FOR UNSAFE PRODUCTS!

Elsie Dominguez was working as a civilian engineer aboard the USNS Carson City in 2021 when she says the ship’s Navy captain, Yamil Sanchez Padilla, raped her in her cabin.

I received the first copies of the newly reissued Yes Symphonic Live album on vinyl, CD, and Blu-ray featuring my illustrations. Street date 1/23/26. I wrote the following for the liner notes:

“For the new cover art, I reimagined (or “magnified”) my original 2002 Symphonic Live cover. In this new edition, we see a prehistoric shaman summoning a Talisman’s power above a vast forest – the energy of its levitating rings opening crop circle style sinkholes in the ground. 

I also created an “alternate cover” that’s a little more intimate, depicting a man and his child watching as a Talisman’s silver rings return to sacred ground overlooking a hazy canyon. As an homage to the great album artist Aubrey “Po” Powell, who masterfully directed the Symphonic Live concert film, I chose to bring back the Hipgnosis treatment of Roger Dean’s Yes logo last seen on the covers of Going For The One and Tormato.

Elsewhere, the gatefold illustration shows four colossal Talisman monuments relaying bolts of energy to open a dimensional rift. Another illustration, “Giant Under The Sun”, is a tribute to Chris Squire, featuring a humpback whale rejoicing before a massive oceanic Talisman.

Late in the process, I decided to have some fun bridging the ancient and modern eras of interdimensional reality, so I created an archival photograph of an early 20th Century explorer’s discovery of a Talisman while it’s partially exposed by melting ice, adapting a public domain photograph by Herbert G. Ponting, circa 1911.

One final note: every composition in this sleeve was modeled, composited, or digitally hand-drawn by me, except for the aforementioned Ponting photo. None of the illustrations were created using AI. However, I used Photoshop’s generative tools to clean-up and composite some of the CG renders.

Thank you to everyone at Mercury Studios for gifting me with the rare privilege of working on this special edition of Symphonic Live, and to Jordan Berliant for initially commissioning my work back in 2001-2002. I’m especially grateful for the support of the Yes fan community.”

“For the new cover art, I reimagined (or “magnified”) my original 2002 Symphonic Live cover. In this new edition, we see a prehistoric shaman summoning a Talisman’s power above a vast forest – the energy of its levitating rings opening crop circle style sinkholes in the ground. 

I also created an “alternate cover” that’s a little more intimate, depicting a man and his child watching as a Talisman’s silver rings return to sacred ground overlooking a hazy canyon. As an homage to the great album artist Aubrey “Po” Powell, who masterfully directed the Symphonic Live concert film, I chose to bring back the Hipgnosis treatment of Roger Dean’s Yes logo last seen on the covers of Going For The One and Tormato.

Elsewhere, the gatefold illustration shows four colossal Talisman monuments relaying bolts of energy to open a dimensional rift. Another illustration, “Giant Under The Sun”, is a tribute to Chris Squire, featuring a humpback whale rejoicing before a massive oceanic Talisman.

Late in the process, I decided to have some fun bridging the ancient and modern eras of interdimensional reality, so I created an archival photograph of an early 20th Century explorer’s discovery of a Talisman while it’s partially exposed by melting ice, adapting a public domain photograph by Herbert G. Ponting, circa 1911.

One final note: every composition in this sleeve was modeled, composited, or digitally hand-drawn by me, except for the aforementioned Ponting photo. None of the illustrations were created using AI. However, I used Photoshop’s generative tools to clean-up and composite some of the CG renders.

Thank you to everyone at Mercury Studios for gifting me with the rare privilege of working on this special edition of Symphonic Live, and to Jordan Berliant for initially commissioning my work back in 2001-2002. I’m especially grateful for the support of the Yes fan community.”

I received the first copies of the newly reissued Yes Symphonic Live album on vinyl, CD, and Blu-ray featuring my illustrations. Street date 1/23/26. I wrote the following for the liner notes:

“For the new cover art, I reimagined (or “magnified”) my original 2002 Symphonic Live cover. In this new edition, we see a prehistoric shaman summoning a Talisman’s power above a vast forest – the energy of its levitating rings opening crop circle style sinkholes in the ground. 

I also created an “alternate cover” that’s a little more intimate, depicting a man and his child watching as a Talisman’s silver rings return to sacred ground overlooking a hazy canyon. As an homage to the great album artist Aubrey “Po” Powell, who masterfully directed the Symphonic Live concert film, I chose to bring back the Hipgnosis treatment of Roger Dean’s Yes logo last seen on the covers of Going For The One and Tormato.

Elsewhere, the gatefold illustration shows four colossal Talisman monuments relaying bolts of energy to open a dimensional rift. Another illustration, “Giant Under The Sun”, is a tribute to Chris Squire, featuring a humpback whale rejoicing before a massive oceanic Talisman.

Late in the process, I decided to have some fun bridging the ancient and modern eras of interdimensional reality, so I created an archival photograph of an early 20th Century explorer’s discovery of a Talisman while it’s partially exposed by melting ice, adapting a public domain photograph by Herbert G. Ponting, circa 1911.

One final note: every composition in this sleeve was modeled, composited, or digitally hand-drawn by me, except for the aforementioned Ponting photo. None of the illustrations were created using AI. However, I used Photoshop’s generative tools to clean-up and composite some of the CG renders.

Thank you to everyone at Mercury Studios for gifting me with the rare privilege of working on this special edition of Symphonic Live, and to Jordan Berliant for initially commissioning my work back in 2001-2002. I’m especially grateful for the support of the Yes fan community.”

In a forceful statement, U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle’s attorneys, Jesse Binnall and David M. Schwartz, categorically reject Eric Deters’ accusations, arguing that his own signed contract and communications contradict his public claims.

As the first woman to serve as U.S. Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle has made American energy security and strategic cooperation defining priorities of her diplomatic mission.
